lessons.title: What Is T-SQL? A Tour of SSMS
Connecting to a Database & the USE Statement

slots.practicalActivity: In SSMS, connect to the local SQL Server instance, open a new query window against AdventureWorks2012, and run USE AdventureWorks2012; then explore Object Explorer and expand Tables, noting at least 8 table names under Person, Sales, and Production schemas. Write and run 3 SELECT TOP 10 * FROM queries against three different tables you found, and use the Results grid, Messages tab, and query execution time indicator to see what each one reports.
slots.deliverable: A saved .sql script with 3 working SELECT TOP 10 * FROM queries against three different AdventureWorks2012 tables, plus a one-line comment above each noting which schema it belongs to.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 5 original SELECT queries against AdventureWorks2012: 2 using SELECT * and 3 selecting specific named columns (at least 3 columns each) from Person.Person, Production.Product, and Sales.SalesOrderHeader.
slots.deliverable: A .sql file with 5 working SELECT queries, each run successfully in SSMS with visible results.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 4 queries against Person.Person that alias at least 2 columns each with AS, and build a full-name output by concatenating FirstName + ' ' + LastName (handling MiddleName with a trailing space) into a single aliased column called FullName.
slots.deliverable: 4 queries producing readable aliased column headers, including one FullName concatenation query.

slots.practicalActivity: Against Production.Product, write one simple CASE expression that translates the Color column into a friendlier label (e.g. 'N/A' for NULL), and one searched CASE expression that buckets ListPrice into 'Budget', 'Mid-range', and 'Premium' using comparison ranges.
slots.deliverable: 2 queries with working CASE expressions, each producing a new derived column in the result set.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3 SELECT DISTINCT queries against Sales.SalesOrderHeader and Person.Person (e.g. distinct TerritoryID values, distinct City values), then reformat 3 of today's earlier queries from this chapter with consistent capitalization, indentation, and a header comment block explaining what each query does.
slots.deliverable: 3 DISTINCT queries plus a cleaned-up, commented version of at least 3 earlier queries from this chapter.

slots.practicalActivity: Combine everything from Chapter 1, T-SQL Foundations: write one original query against AdventureWorks2012 that selects specific aliased columns from Person.Person, concatenates a full name, adds a CASE-based label column, and applies DISTINCT — all in a single statement, fully commented.
slots.deliverable: One well-commented original query combining column aliasing, string concatenation, CASE, and DISTINCT in a single SELECT statement.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 5 WHERE-clause queries against Sales.SalesOrderHeader and Production.Product using comparison operators (=, <>, >, <, >=, <=) to filter on OrderDate, TotalDue, and ListPrice.
slots.deliverable: 5 filtered queries, each returning a different subset of rows, with the row count noted in a comment for each.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3 queries combining AND/OR/NOT conditions against Person.Person and Production.Product (e.g. products that are red OR blue AND under $500), then write 3 LIKE queries using %, _, and NOT LIKE against LastName or Name columns.
slots.deliverable: 6 queries demonstrating compound boolean filters and wildcard pattern matches.

lessons.title: Handling NULL (IS NULL / IS NOT NULL)

slots.practicalActivity: Write 2 IN queries and 2 BETWEEN queries against Sales.SalesOrderHeader (e.g. specific TerritoryIDs, OrderDate ranges), then write 2 queries using IS NULL / IS NOT NULL against Person.Person.MiddleName and Production.Product.Color.
slots.deliverable: 6 queries covering IN, BETWEEN, and NULL-safe filtering, each verified to return correct rows in SSMS.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3 ORDER BY queries (ascending, descending, and multi-column sort) against Sales.SalesOrderHeader, then write 2 TOP queries (one TOP N, one TOP N PERCENT) to find the highest-value orders.
slots.deliverable: 5 queries demonstrating sorting and TOP/TOP PERCENT limiting on real order data.

lessons.title: Predicates: How SQL Server Filters Data

slots.practicalActivity: Find a column with duplicate values (e.g. ListPrice in Production.Product) and write a TOP WITH TIES query ordered by that column; then write 2 queries comparing how SQL Server evaluates predicates on an indexed column filter vs. a non-indexed column filter, using SET STATISTICS IO ON to see the difference.
slots.deliverable: A TOP WITH TIES query returning tied rows, plus 2 predicate-comparison queries with STATISTICS IO output captured.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one combined query against AdventureWorks2012's Sales.SalesOrderHeader that filters with a compound WHERE (AND/OR/IN/BETWEEN), handles NULLs safely, sorts the result, and returns only the TOP 10 WITH TIES — simulating a real 'top customers by order value' report, closing out the Filtering and Sorting chapter.
slots.deliverable: One original multi-clause query combining filtering, NULL handling, sorting, and TOP WITH TIES, with a 2-sentence comment explaining the business question it answers.

slots.practicalActivity: Identify the primary key and foreign key columns linking Sales.SalesOrderHeader to Sales.Customer and Person.Person using Object Explorer's Keys folders, then write 2 INNER JOIN queries: SalesOrderHeader to Customer, and Customer to Person, returning customer names with their order totals.
slots.deliverable: 2 INNER JOIN queries returning combined customer-and-order data, plus a short note identifying the PK/FK pair used in each join.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a LEFT JOIN from Production.Product to Sales.SalesOrderDetail to find products that have never been ordered (check for NULL on the right side), then rewrite the same logic as a RIGHT JOIN with the table order swapped to confirm it returns the same result set.
slots.deliverable: A LEFT JOIN query listing never-ordered products, plus an equivalent RIGHT JOIN query proving the same result from the opposite table order.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a FULL OUTER JOIN between two related AdventureWorks2012 tables to surface unmatched rows on both sides, then write a CROSS JOIN between a small distinct lookup set (e.g. distinct Sizes from Production.Product) and Production.Product to generate every combination, calculating the expected row count before running it.
slots.deliverable: A FULL OUTER JOIN showing unmatched rows from both tables, and a CROSS JOIN query whose actual row count you verify against your pre-calculated rows(A) x rows(B) estimate.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a SELF JOIN against a table with a self-referencing or hierarchical relationship in AdventureWorks2012 (e.g. Sales.SalesPerson territory structure) to pair related rows, then write a 3-table JOIN chaining Sales.SalesOrderHeader, Sales.SalesOrderDetail, and Production.Product to list order line items with real product names.
slots.deliverable: A working SELF JOIN query and a 3-table JOIN query returning order line items with real product names.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a CROSS APPLY query that, for each customer in Sales.Customer, returns their top 3 highest-value orders from Sales.SalesOrderHeader using a correlated TOP subquery inside the APPLY clause; then convert it to OUTER APPLY and compare which customers (if any) with zero orders now appear.
slots.deliverable: A CROSS APPLY 'top-3-orders-per-customer' query and its OUTER APPLY variant, with a one-line comparison of the row-count difference.

slots.practicalActivity: For 4 different business questions you write yourself (e.g. 'all products and whether they've sold', 'every order with customer info', 'all possible product/territory pairs for planning'), decide which join type fits each and write the query, annotating each with a comment justifying the join choice.
slots.deliverable: 4 queries, each preceded by a comment explaining why that specific join type (INNER/LEFT/CROSS/etc.) was the right choice for the question.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Joining Tables: without looking back at lesson examples, write an original 5-table join query from scratch (SalesOrderHeader, SalesOrderDetail, Product, Customer, Person) that lists, for every order, the customer's full name, product name, quantity, and line total — deliberately choosing INNER vs. LEFT JOIN for each relationship and documenting the choice in comments.
slots.deliverable: One original 5-table join lab query with full comments justifying each join type, executed successfully with results visible in SSMS.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 2 COUNT queries (COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT column)) against Sales.SalesOrderDetail, and 2 SUM/AVG queries computing the total and average LineTotal across the whole table.
slots.deliverable: 4 aggregate queries returning single summary numbers from real order-detail data.

slots.practicalActivity: Write MIN/MAX queries finding the cheapest and most expensive product in Production.Product, then write 3 single-column GROUP BY queries: total sales per ProductID, order count per CustomerID, and average price per ProductSubcategoryID.
slots.deliverable: 2 MIN/MAX queries and 3 single-column GROUP BY aggregate queries.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a GROUP BY query grouping Sales.SalesOrderDetail by both ProductID and SpecialOfferID, then write 2 queries contrasting HAVING (filtering on the aggregate, e.g. products with total quantity sold > 500) vs. WHERE (filtering rows before aggregation) on the same data.
slots.deliverable: A multi-column GROUP BY query plus a side-by-side WHERE-vs-HAVING comparison on the same aggregate.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a UNION query combining two differently-filtered SELECTs from Sales.SalesOrderHeader (e.g. big orders and small orders) and the same query as UNION ALL, comparing row counts and duplicate handling; then write a VAR/STDEV query on SalesOrderHeader.TotalDue.
slots.deliverable: A UNION and UNION ALL pair showing the duplicate-removal difference, plus one VAR/STDEV statistical query.

slots.practicalActivity: Build an original summary-report query combining GROUP BY, HAVING, and at least 2 aggregate functions to answer: 'which product subcategories had total sales over a threshold you choose, ranked by total descending?'
slots.deliverable: One polished summary-report query with GROUP BY, HAVING, and ORDER BY producing a ranked business report.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Grouping and Aggregating: write an original sales-summary report from scratch, joining Sales.SalesOrderHeader to Sales.SalesOrderDetail and Production.Product, grouping by product category, using COUNT/SUM/AVG together, filtering groups with HAVING, and sorting the final report — combining join skills from Chapter 3 with aggregation from this chapter.
slots.deliverable: One original multi-table aggregate report query combining joins, GROUP BY, HAVING, and multiple aggregate functions.

slots.practicalActivity: Inspect the column data types of Person.Person and Production.ProductDescription (via Object Explorer's table Design view or sys.columns) to find real CHAR, VARCHAR, and NVARCHAR columns; then write 2 queries using DATALENGTH() to compare how a CHAR column, a VARCHAR column, and an NVARCHAR column each store the same short text value, noting the byte-size difference Unicode adds.
slots.deliverable: 2 DATALENGTH() comparison queries against real Person.Person/Production.ProductDescription columns, plus written notes on which columns use CHAR, VARCHAR, and NVARCHAR and why the byte sizes differ.

slots.practicalActivity: Find a VARCHAR(MAX) column in Production.ProductDescription and write a query returning its DATALENGTH() to confirm it can exceed the 8,000-byte VARCHAR limit; then write 2 queries using LEN, UPPER, and LOWER against Person.Person.LastName to standardize casing and measure name lengths.
slots.deliverable: A VARCHAR(MAX) length-verification query, plus 2 LEN/UPPER/LOWER queries against real last-name data.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 2 SUBSTRING/CHARINDEX queries that dynamically extract a segment of a Production.Product.ProductNumber code by locating its '-' separator with CHARINDEX; then write a STUFF query that masks part of a text value and a REPLACE query that swaps a character in Production.Product.Name, comparing what each function changes.
slots.deliverable: 2 SUBSTRING/CHARINDEX extraction queries plus a STUFF-vs-REPLACE comparison pair, all run against real Production.Product data.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 3 TRIM/LTRIM/RTRIM queries cleaning whitespace from a concatenated name column, proving the before/after difference with LEN(); then query sys.columns (or Object Explorer) to find 3 real date/time columns in Sales.SalesOrderHeader and note their exact data types (e.g. datetime vs. date).
slots.deliverable: 3 trimming queries with LEN()-verified before/after whitespace proof, plus a written list of 3 real date/time columns and their data types.

slots.practicalActivity: Write 4 GETDATE/DATEADD/DATEDIFF queries against Sales.SalesOrderHeader computing order age in days, a projected ship date, and orders placed within the last 30 days relative to the dataset's latest OrderDate; then write 3 CAST/CONVERT queries reformatting OrderDate into different string styles and converting a numeric column to varchar for concatenation.
slots.deliverable: 4 working date-function queries plus 3 CAST/CONVERT formatting queries, all against real order dates.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a scratch temp table seeded with intentionally duplicated rows copied from Production.Product, then write a dedup query using ROW_NUMBER() or GROUP BY to identify and remove the duplicates, verifying the row count before and after.
slots.deliverable: One working duplicate-removal query tested against a scratch table with real duplicate rows, with before/after row counts noted.

slots.practicalActivity: Build one original data-cleaning query for Chapter 5, Data Types, Strings, and Dates: pull Person.Person names, TRIM any whitespace, UPPER-case the last name, concatenate a formatted full name, CONVERT a date column to 'yyyy-mm-dd' string format, and use SUBSTRING to pull the first 3 characters of a phone number — all in one SELECT.
slots.deliverable: One combined string/date-cleaning query exercising at least 5 different functions from this chapter.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a single-value (scalar) subquery finding all products priced above the average ListPrice, then write a multi-value subquery using IN to find all orders placed by customers in a specific list of territories returned by a subquery against Sales.SalesTerritory.
slots.deliverable: A scalar-subquery 'above average price' query and a multi-value IN subquery query.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a correlated subquery that returns each customer's most recent order date inline per row, then write an EXISTS query finding customers who have placed at least one order over $5,000, and a NOT EXISTS query finding products never ordered.
slots.deliverable: One correlated subquery and two EXISTS/NOT EXISTS queries, each verified against known AdventureWorks2012 data.

slots.practicalActivity: Rewrite one of your earlier subquery solutions as a CTE for readability, then write a recursive CTE that walks the Production.ProductCategory/ProductSubcategory hierarchy to list parent-child levels.
slots.deliverable: A readable CTE rewrite of a prior query, plus a working recursive CTE traversing a real hierarchy in AdventureWorks2012.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a view named vw_CustomerOrderSummary that joins Customer, Person, and SalesOrderHeader to show each customer's order count and total spend, then query it like a table; research via sys.indexes whether an indexed view would suit this case and explain why or why not in a comment.
slots.deliverable: A working CREATE VIEW statement, a SELECT against that view, and a written note on indexed-view suitability.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a PIVOT query turning Sales.SalesOrderHeader order counts by TerritoryID into columns, one column per territory, with order years as rows; then write an UNPIVOT query that reshapes that same wide result back into a tall/normalized format, confirming the row count matches the original pre-pivot data.
slots.deliverable: A working PIVOT query reshaping territory-by-year order data into a cross-tab layout, plus an UNPIVOT query that reverses it back into normalized rows.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Subqueries, CTEs, and Views: build one query that uses a CTE to pre-aggregate order totals per customer, uses EXISTS against that CTE to filter to customers above a threshold, then PIVOTs the result by order year — combining CTEs, EXISTS, and PIVOT in a single original multi-step query.
slots.deliverable: One original multi-technique query chaining a CTE, an EXISTS filter, and a PIVOT, successfully executed in SSMS.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a script that DECLAREs 3 variables of different types (INT, VARCHAR, DATETIME), assigns values with SELECT/SET, and PRINTs a formatted message using them; split the script into 2 batches with GO and confirm the variables don't persist across the GO boundary.
slots.deliverable: A script demonstrating variable declaration and use, plus proof (via an error or empty result) that GO resets variable scope.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a script that stores a real product's ListPrice (via SELECT INTO a variable) and uses IF/ELSE with BEGIN/END blocks to PRINT different messages for 'budget', 'mid-range', and 'premium' price tiers.
slots.deliverable: A working IF/ELSE/BEGIN/END script that branches based on a real queried value.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a WHILE loop that prints the numbers 1-10 with a running total, then write a cursor that iterates over the top 5 highest-priced products in Production.Product and PRINTs each product's name and price one row at a time.
slots.deliverable: A working WHILE loop script and a working cursor script that iterates real product rows.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a stored procedure usp_GetCustomerOrders that takes a @CustomerID parameter and returns that customer's orders from Sales.SalesOrderHeader, with a default parameter value and an OUTPUT parameter returning the order count; then EXEC it with 2 different customer IDs.
slots.deliverable: A working CREATE PROCEDURE with input and OUTPUT parameters, executed successfully with 2 different inputs.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a dynamic SQL script using sp_executesql that builds a SELECT statement where the filter column's value is chosen based on a variable, using parameterized dynamic SQL (not string concatenation of user input) to avoid injection risk; then create a small staging temp table with a few changed and new product rows and write a MERGE statement that syncs it into a scratch copy of Production.Product (INSERT new rows, UPDATE changed rows), verifying the row-by-row outcome afterward.
slots.deliverable: One working sp_executesql script with properly parameterized dynamic SQL, plus a MERGE statement with INSERT and UPDATE actions tested against a staging table.

slots.practicalActivity: Build one original stored procedure for Chapter 7, Programming with T-SQL: accept a @MinTotal parameter, use IF/ELSE to validate it, and return orders above that total using proper BEGIN/END and parameter handling — then EXEC it twice with different threshold values.
slots.deliverable: One original parameterized stored procedure combining variables, IF/ELSE, and BEGIN/END, executed with 2 different parameter values.

slots.practicalActivity: On a scratch copy of a small table, write a script using BEGIN TRANSACTION, make an UPDATE, verify the change inside the transaction, then ROLLBACK and verify it reverted; repeat with COMMIT and verify the change persists. Write one sentence per ACID property explaining how this demo illustrated it.
slots.deliverable: A working transaction script demonstrating both ROLLBACK and COMMIT outcomes, plus 4 short written ACID explanations tied to the demo.

slots.practicalActivity: Open two SSMS query windows against the same scratch table: in window 1, start a transaction with an UPDATE but don't commit; in window 2, try to SELECT or UPDATE the same rows and observe the blocking; use sp_who2 or sys.dm_tran_locks to inspect the lock held, then COMMIT window 1 and confirm window 2 unblocks.
slots.deliverable: A documented two-session blocking demo with notes on the lock type observed and how it resolved.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a TRY/CATCH block around an intentionally failing statement (e.g. an INSERT violating a constraint), capturing ERROR_MESSAGE/ERROR_NUMBER in the CATCH block; then write a script using RAISERROR and one using THROW to raise a custom business-rule error.
slots.deliverable: A working TRY/CATCH script that captures a real error, plus one RAISERROR and one THROW example raising custom errors.

slots.practicalActivity: In SSMS's connection dialog, examine the difference between Windows Authentication and SQL Server Authentication options; query sys.server_principals to list the login accounts and their authentication type on your instance, and write a short note on when you'd choose each mode in a real deployment.
slots.deliverable: A query result listing server logins by auth type, plus a short written recommendation for a given deployment scenario.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for Transactions and Error Handling: write one script combining a transaction, TRY/CATCH, and THROW — attempt an UPDATE inside BEGIN TRANSACTION, deliberately trigger a constraint violation, catch it, ROLLBACK inside the CATCH block, and THROW a custom re-raised error with a clear message.
slots.deliverable: One original script combining transactions, TRY/CATCH, ROLLBACK, and THROW into a safe error-handling pattern.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a query using OVER(PARTITION BY TerritoryID) to show each order's TotalDue alongside the average TotalDue for its territory; then write a ROW_NUMBER() query numbering each customer's orders from most recent to oldest, partitioned by CustomerID.
slots.deliverable: A PARTITION BY aggregate-window query and a ROW_NUMBER() per-customer ordering query.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a query ranking products by ListPrice within each ProductSubcategoryID using both RANK() and DENSE_RANK(), comparing how they handle tied prices; then write an NTILE(4) query splitting customers into spending quartiles based on total order value.
slots.deliverable: A side-by-side RANK vs. DENSE_RANK query showing tie behavior, plus an NTILE(4) quartile-assignment query.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Window and Ranking Functions: build an original 'top 3 products per category by sales' report using ROW_NUMBER() PARTITION BY category ORDER BY total sales descending inside a CTE, filtering WHERE rn <= 3 in the outer query — a classic real-world window-function pattern.
slots.deliverable: One original top-N-per-group report query using a window function inside a CTE, correctly limited to the top 3 rows per category.

lessons.title: The Cartesian Product: What Happens When Joins Go Wrong

slots.practicalActivity: Write a baseline query against Sales.SalesOrderDetail and time it using SSMS's query execution time; then deliberately write a query that omits the JOIN condition between two tables to produce an accidental Cartesian product, observe the exploded row count, then fix it by adding the correct ON clause.
slots.deliverable: A timed baseline query, plus a before/after pair showing an accidental Cartesian product and its corrected join.

lessons.title: Joins vs. Subqueries: Which Is Faster, and Why
EXISTS vs. IN vs. JOIN for Existence Checks

slots.practicalActivity: Write the question 'customers with at least one order over $5,000' three ways: as a JOIN with DISTINCT, as an IN subquery, and as an EXISTS subquery; turn on Include Actual Execution Plan and compare the plans and relative costs of all three.
slots.deliverable: Three functionally-equivalent queries (JOIN, IN, EXISTS) with execution-plan cost notes comparing them.

lessons.title: Clustered vs. Nonclustered Indexes: Choosing Wisely

slots.practicalActivity: Write a non-SARGable query (e.g. WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2013) and a SARGable rewrite (WHERE OrderDate >= '2013-01-01' AND OrderDate < '2014-01-01') against Sales.SalesOrderHeader, comparing execution plans; then use Object Explorer to identify the clustered vs. nonclustered indexes on that table.
slots.deliverable: A non-SARGable/SARGable query pair with plan comparison, plus a written list of the table's clustered and nonclustered indexes.

lessons.title: Reading Execution Plans: Scans vs. Seeks

slots.practicalActivity: Create a filtered index on Sales.SalesOrderHeader for a narrow condition (e.g. WHERE Status = 5) with an included column, then write a query that benefits from it and confirm via the execution plan that the filtered index is used (Index Seek) rather than a full scan.
slots.deliverable: A CREATE INDEX statement (filtered, with INCLUDE), plus execution-plan notes confirming an Index Seek on it.

lessons.title: SET STATISTICS TIME and IO in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: Turn on SET STATISTICS TIME ON and SET STATISTICS IO ON, run 2 versions of the same query (one aided by an index, one forced to scan), and compare CPU time and logical reads; then capture the XML execution plan for one of them.
slots.deliverable: Before/after STATISTICS TIME/IO output comparing two query versions, plus one captured XML execution plan.

lessons.title: Temp Tables vs. Table Variables vs. CTEs: Performance Tradeoffs

slots.practicalActivity: Solve the same multi-step aggregation problem three ways: once staging intermediate results in a #temp table, once in a table variable, and once in a CTE, comparing execution plans and noting where each approach's performance differs; then find and fix 2 performance anti-patterns in queries you wrote earlier in this course (e.g. SELECT *, a non-SARGable WHERE, a scalar function on a filtered column) by rewriting each one and comparing before/after execution plans.
slots.deliverable: Three equivalent query solutions (temp table, table variable, CTE) with written performance notes, plus 2 before/after anti-pattern rewrites with plan or STATISTICS IO evidence of improvement.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Performance Tuning: pick 2 queries from earlier chapters and apply the full tuning checklist from this chapter to each — check SARGability, index usage, anti-patterns, and compare a temp-table/CTE approach — writing a short tuning report for each with a final optimization recommendation.
slots.deliverable: A short written tuning report for 2 prior queries, each covering SARGability, index usage, and a final optimization recommendation.

slots.practicalActivity: In Object Explorer, expand the Keys folder for Production.Product and Sales.SalesOrderHeader to identify their real primary and foreign keys; then write a CREATE TABLE script for a small scratch table with an explicit PRIMARY KEY and a FOREIGN KEY referencing an existing AdventureWorks2012 table, and test that an INSERT violating the foreign key fails.
slots.deliverable: A CREATE TABLE script with a PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY, plus a failed INSERT proving the foreign-key constraint is enforced.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a UNIQUE constraint on a non-key column of your scratch table, then add a NOT NULL constraint and a CHECK constraint (e.g. CHECK quantity > 0); test each one by attempting an INSERT that violates it and confirming SQL Server rejects it.
slots.deliverable: A scratch table with UNIQUE, NOT NULL, and CHECK constraints, plus 3 failed INSERT attempts proving each constraint is enforced.

slots.practicalActivity: Identify one real one-to-one relationship and one real one-to-many relationship in AdventureWorks2012's schema (e.g. a one-to-one between an order header and its shipping detail, and a one-to-many between Sales.Customer and Sales.SalesOrderHeader), and write a query proving each with a JOIN and a row-count check.
slots.deliverable: 2 queries proving a real one-to-one and a real one-to-many relationship in the schema, each with a row-count comparison.

slots.practicalActivity: Find the many-to-many relationship between Production.Product and Sales.SalesOrderHeader via the Sales.SalesOrderDetail junction table and write a query proving it; then sketch a deliberately unnormalized flat table (e.g. an order with repeating product columns) and write out, in comments, how you'd split it to satisfy 1NF.
slots.deliverable: A junction-table query proving a many-to-many relationship, plus a written 1NF normalization walkthrough of a deliberately denormalized example.

slots.practicalActivity: Continue the 1NF example from the previous slot through 2NF and 3NF in comments, showing how partial and transitive dependencies get split into separate tables; then, in Object Explorer, expand System Databases and write one sentence each on the real purpose of master, msdb, tempdb, and model.
slots.deliverable: A written 2NF/3NF continuation of the earlier normalization example, plus a one-sentence-each summary of the 4 system databases.

slots.practicalActivity: Create both a #LocalTemp and a ##GlobalTemp table and, from a second query window, confirm you can see the global one but not the local one; then capture a trace of one of your queries running with SQL Server Profiler or Extended Events.
slots.deliverable: A local/global temp table visibility test across two sessions, plus a captured Profiler/Extended Events trace of a real query execution.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for Database Design Fundamentals: design and create, with CREATE TABLE, a small 3-table normalized schema from scratch for a new business scenario (e.g. tracking product warranty claims), including PK/FK/UNIQUE/CHECK constraints and at least one one-to-many relationship, then insert sample rows and query across all 3 tables with a JOIN.
slots.deliverable: A working 3-table CREATE TABLE schema with proper constraints and relationships, populated with sample data and queried with a JOIN.

lessons.title: OLTP vs. OLAP: Two Different Worlds

slots.practicalActivity: Compare AdventureWorks2012 (OLTP) and AdventureWorksDW2014 (OLAP/warehouse) side by side in Object Explorer: note how table counts and naming (Fact/Dim prefixes) differ; connect to AdventureWorksDW2014 and run SELECT TOP 20 against DimCustomer and FactInternetSales, writing a short comparison versus the OLTP tables.
slots.deliverable: A written side-by-side comparison of AdventureWorks2012 vs. AdventureWorksDW2014 structure, plus 2 exploratory SELECT queries against the warehouse database.

slots.practicalActivity: In AdventureWorksDW2014, identify whether any tables look scoped to a single department (a potential data mart) versus the full enterprise warehouse; then write a short comparison (in a comment block) of how a raw, unstructured data lake would differ from the structured, modeled warehouse you're querying.
slots.deliverable: A written comparison of data mart vs. data lake vs. the AdventureWorksDW2014 warehouse you're working in, grounded in its real table structure.

lessons.title: Data Warehouse vs. Data Lake vs. Data Mart

slots.practicalActivity: Write a mini ETL-style script: SELECT raw rows from AdventureWorks2012's Sales.SalesOrderHeader, transform them (aggregate by month), and INSERT the transformed result into a new scratch summary table — demonstrating Extract-Transform-Load in T-SQL; then write one sentence contrasting this ETL approach with an ELT approach that would load the raw rows first and transform them afterward inside the warehouse.
slots.deliverable: A working mini-ETL script that extracts, transforms, and loads data into a new table, plus a written ETL-vs-ELT comparison.

slots.practicalActivity: In AdventureWorksDW2014, identify FactInternetSales and at least 3 related Dim tables, then write a query that JOINs the fact table to all 3 dimension tables to produce a readable sales report — a classic star-schema query.
slots.deliverable: A star-schema JOIN query combining FactInternetSales with 3 dimension tables into a readable report.

slots.practicalActivity: Check whether any dimension in AdventureWorksDW2014 is snowflaked (joined to a sub-dimension) and write what you find; then query DimCustomer for StartDate/EndDate or current-flag columns to check whether it shows a Slowly Changing Dimension (SCD Type 2) pattern.
slots.deliverable: A written note on any snowflaked dimension structure found, plus a written finding on whether DimCustomer shows an SCD Type 2 pattern.

lessons.title: Where T-SQL Fits in the BI/Warehousing Pipeline

slots.practicalActivity: Query DimCustomer in AdventureWorksDW2014 and identify its surrogate key column versus its natural/business key column (e.g. CustomerAlternateKey); then write a one-paragraph summary placing T-SQL's role in a BI pipeline relative to tools like SSIS and Power BI.
slots.deliverable: A written identification of DimCustomer's surrogate vs. natural key columns, plus a short summary of T-SQL's role in the BI pipeline.

slots.practicalActivity: Course capstone lab: using AdventureWorksDW2014, write one original multi-dimension star-schema query joining FactInternetSales to at least 3 Dim tables, apply a window function (RANK or ROW_NUMBER) to find the top 5 customers by sales per year, and wrap the whole thing in a CTE — combining warehouse concepts, joins, and window functions from across this entire course into one final query.
slots.deliverable: One original capstone query combining a star-schema join, a CTE, and a window function to produce a 'top 5 customers per year' report from the data warehouse.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can write and tune real T-SQL -- filtering, joining, aggregating, subqueries/CTEs, stored procedures, transactions, and window functions -- against live SQL Server databases, and can read and query a star-schema data warehouse.
